architecture.mechanism: Cyclic variation of external parameters can extract ensemble-average energy from a chaotic, non-integrable two-degree-of-freedom system, with symmetry breaking enabling the energy decrement.
architecture.intervention: Apply a controlled cyclic modulation of an external vehicle parameter (e.g., throttle plate position via the electronic throttle control, or alternator/voltage-setpoint cycling tied to the ETCS duty cycle) in synchrony with the idle/acceleration event window, using a calibrated cycle amplitude/frequency to bias the engine's internal energy state downward when unintended high-RPM conditions are detected.
architecture.expected_effect: During a detected unintended-revving event, the cyclic parameter modulation lowers the ensemble-average energy delivered to the drivetrain, reducing the runaway RPM surge and forcing a controlled return to idle, thereby preventing the subsequent sudden stall rather than allowing open-loop acceleration.
architecture.falsification_test: On a dynamometer, repeatedly trigger the unintended-revving fault condition (disconnected pedal sensor signal, simulated) with the intervention disabled vs. enabled across ≥30 trials; record peak RPM, time-to-stall, and whether a controlled stall (RPM ramp-down to commanded idle) occurs. If the enabled-intervention trials do not show a statistically significant reduction in peak RPM and a controlled descent to idle versus the disabled trials (e.g., paired t-test p<0.05, ≥30% reduction in peak surge RPM), the mechanism is falsified for this application.
